segments.text: Compressed gas cylinders, major and minor leaks.
To help prevent leaks in your compressed gas cylinders,
remove rusty, corroded and damaged cylinders from servers
before they develop a leak.
Return cylinders when they are no longer used
or if they are more than 10 years past
the last test state stamped on the cylinder.
A minor compressed gas leak is a small, slow
and controllable release of an inert,
not asphyxiating or other low hazard gas.
That poses a low risk of personal injury
or exposure.
A major compressed gas leak is a large,
uncontrollable release of gas that constitutes
a serious hazard to laboratory occupants,
facilities or the environment.
A small leak in a toxic or highly hazardous cylinder
is also considered a major leak.
If a minor leak is detected, notify people in the area.
If you have not already done so, don appropriate PPE.
Determine that the leak is coming from the cylinder
and cannot be fixed by tightening connections
or valve components.
Then move the cylinder into a fume hood
under a local exhaust canopy
or to an isolated, well-ventilated area to vent
if it is safe to do so.
If the gas is flammable or oxidizing,
remove any nearby and combustible materials.
Evacuate the immediate area and post warning signs
to prevent access by others.
Notify the laboratory supervisor and EH&S of the incident.
Remain outside the immediate area
until the cylinder contents have been exhausted.
Return the cylinder to the supplier for needed repairs.
When a major leak occurs, including small leaks
of toxic or highly hazardous gases,
evacuate the area and activate the building
fire or chemical spill alarm.
Call 911 and EH&S to report the incidents.
Provide emergency response officials
with details of the incident upon their arrival.
Report all accidents, incidents and near misses
to the ISU incident portal.
For more information about gas cylinders,
check out the Gas Cylinder Safety Guidelines
manual linked below.
If you have questions, please contact ISU EH&S.
